This summer, the Australian Bureau of Meteorology released a set of maps that might not seem like much at first glance. But in fact, they are a huge step forward for the country. They’re the first national crop maps for Australia, and they’ll be updated every year.
This map of Australia shows the extent of cropland for 2018. (Image: Australian Bureau of Meteorology)
Cropland is defined not just by what it looks like on a particular day, but by what it does over time. So these maps will allow the country to watch as its fields change: to see cropland expand, to see it abandoned, to see it converted to urban use. Repeated visits by analysts will let them capture the land’s change through the growing season. The maps can be refreshed as new imagery arrives, so the country will be able to watch its cropland change again next year, and the year after that, and so on.
Maps like these are essential. Cropland change is important for long-term resource planning. Estimating food production requires knowing how much land is cultivated and where. Better maps give decision-makers a clearer, more consistent picture of the land they’re working with. And the maps also feed into models of yield, harvest forecasts, and early warning systems for shortfalls.
The central bet of the 2018 study was that a single approach mapping both countries well could travel to other regions.
But the maps aren’t just important. They’re also practical, repeatable, and affordable. Which is surprising, because mapping cropland is hard. It’s hard because cropland is defined as much by what it does over time as by its appearance on a single date. It’s hard because you can’t always tell cropland apart from other land cover. It’s hard because reference samples are costly to collect over large areas. And it’s hard because keeping training and test sets independent is essential for an honest accuracy estimate.
For years, those barriers kept many teams from even attempting such work. But the 2018 study by Teluguntla and colleagues demonstrated that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible—without well-resourced agencies. The results? A binary map distinguishing cropland from everything else, produced separately for each country and assessed against independent reference data.
The study used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE). Landsat-8 offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas. Landsat’s multiple spectral bands, plus derived measures such as vegetation indices, supplied features that describe the surface. And GEE hosts the Landsat archive alongside other datasets and runs computation on Google’s cloud infrastructure. Compositing, feature extraction, classification, and accuracy assessment can all happen in GEE, and the analysis can be written once and executed across enormous areas without moving the data.
The study also used a random forest classifier, a machine learning technique that’s not the newest, but that indicates which input variables matter most, helping researchers understand what the model uses to separate cropland from other land cover. The technique copes well with many input variables, tolerates noisy data, and is relatively resistant to overfitting.
In addition, a single pixel at 250 m to 1 km can be a mix of crops, fallow land, trees, roads, and buildings. Pixel mixing makes it hard to determine the extent of cropland where fields are small, such as much of China.
The study used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE) to map cropland in Australia (top) and China (bottom). The output was a binary map distinguishing cropland from everything else, produced separately for each country and assessed against independent reference data. (Image: Teluguntla et al., 2018, ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing)
The results were encouraging. The same code could be pointed at a different region with relatively little modification. And the model could cope with many input variables, tolerate noisy data, and be relatively resistant to overfitting. The central bet of the study was that a method that behaved predictably across very different landscapes would be easier to scale than one needing recalibration for each region.
In addition, the study demonstrated that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies. In 2018, a study by Teluguntla and colleagues was published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing. They used Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE) to map cropland in Australia (top) and China (bottom). The output was a binary map distinguishing cropland from everything else, produced separately for each country and assessed against independent reference data.
Australia and China are sharply different in cropping systems, climates, and landscapes. Yet the study showed that the same approach could map both well. That’s the central bet of the study: that a single approach mapping both countries well could travel to other regions. And if it can, then continent-scale cropland mapping at field-level detail is practical, repeatable, and affordable.
Landsat’s multiple spectral bands, plus derived measures such as vegetation indices, supplied features that describe the surface. (Image: NASA’s Earth Observatory)
These results are especially important for China. The country feeds a huge population from a comparatively small area of farmland, much of it in fragmented, intensively managed plots. In addition, water allocation is a constant concern in Australia. Agriculture is the largest consumer of freshwater globally, and knowing the cropland footprint helps estimate irrigation demand, assess pressure on river basins and aquifers, and target water management.

High-resolution cropland extent maps: how Landsat makes accurate continental mapping possible
The random forest machine learning algorithm generated new cropland extent maps for Australia and China.
When it comes to estimating food production, we need to know how much land is being cultivated, and where. Cropland maps can capture the individual farm fields, whether small or large. But croplands are not defined by their appearance on a single date; they are defined by what they do over time as well as by their appearance on that date. So mapping high resolution (30-m or better) cropland extent over continents, large countries or regions accurately, precisely, repeatedly and rapidly is of great importance for addressing the global food and water security challenges. Unfortunately, many earlier global land cover products used imagery at 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution. This coarse resolution of satellite pixels often results in cropland maps that disagree with one another, use coarse satellite pixels, or depend on national statistics that arrive late and vary in quality.
But Landsat-8 offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas. The data revisits each location about every 16 days. Repeat visits let us capture land change through the growing season. And the multiple spectral bands and derived measures such as vegetation indices supply features describing the surface. So we can build a classification using a pixel-based supervised random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) executed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform. Our study used eight bands of Landsat-8 16-day Operational Land Imager (OLI) data: blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, TIR1, and NDVI. The data covered the years 2013–2015.
Machine learning algorithms like random forest are robust, fast to train, and don’t demand extensive tuning. Random forest builds many decision trees on random subsets of the data and features and combines their votes. It copes well with many input variables, tolerates noisy data, and is relatively resistant to overfitting. Keeping our training and test sets independent is essential for an honest accuracy estimate. So we obtained reference training and validation data from field visits, sub-meter to 5-m very high spatial resolution imagery (VHRI), and ancillary sources such as National agriculture bureaus. We then used a pixel-based supervised random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) executed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform.
We produced high-accuracy, 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China. Our Australian cropland product had overall accuracy of 97.6% and the cropland class had user’s accuracy of 79% (errors of commissions = 21%). Our China cropland product had overall accuracy of 97.5% and the cropland class had user’s accuracy of 84.2% (errors of commissions = 15.8%).
As imagery arrives, our results can be refreshed. Repeat visits over time reveal cropland expansion, abandonment, and conversion to urban use. Cloud cover can limit usable observations in some regions and seasons. But Landsat revisits each location about every 16 days, and its multiple spectral bands and derived measures such as vegetation indices supply features describing the surface. We write our analysis once and execute it across enormous areas without moving the data.
Our 2018 study demonstrated that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies. Landsat data helps us know how much land is cultivated and where. We can estimate food production. We can estimate irrigation demand and assess the pressure on river basins and aquifers. We can target water management. We can help address global food and water security challenges.

Our Plan
The Kampala organization working in these communities has proposed free, safe, community-run resource centers where poor and orphaned children can play, learn, eat, and get basic health care. The centers would offer the following:
- nutrition training on how to feed infants and children well on a tight budget using locally available foods
- safe-motherhood education on prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, and newborn care, especially for young and first-time mothers
- a regular, balanced, nutritious meals
- secure, supervised play spaces that keep children away from the dangers of the street
- age-appropriate early learning activities that build literacy, numeracy, and social skills
- vocational and small-business skills training leading to more stable income and greater independence
The plan is a network of community resource centers built inside or next to the neighborhoods they serve. Each center is meant to be a welcoming, protected space that is free to use and open to the children who need it most. It is meant to be a place where the children who live in these communities can come to play, learn, eat, and get basic health care. The proposal relies on a network of partners to extend what each center can do, but insists on community ownership, with centers meant to belong to the neighborhood.
We are treating caregivers as partners, with parents, guardians, local leaders, and youth helping plan, run, and oversee each center. Caregivers work long hours or are away from home, so young children are often unsupervised. The centers would provide regular, balanced, nutritious meals, basic health care (growth monitoring, immunization follow-up, deworming, first aid, referrals to clinics and hospitals), and safe-motherhood education (prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, newborn care, especially for young and first-time mothers), and provide secure, supervised play spaces away from the dangers of the street.
The centers would also provide age-appropriate early learning activities that build literacy, numeracy, and social skills, offer nutrition training on how to feed infants and children well on a tight budget using locally available foods, and provide vocational and small-business skills training leading to more stable income and greater independence. They would also provide regular, balanced, nutritious meals.
Our Partners
We are looking for supporters who can share our vision, partner by offering their services, expertise, or resources, and support the work financially. NGOs, faith-based groups, and businesses can provide expertise, materials, training opportunities, or funding. Local government and community structures can align the centers with public services and child-protection systems. Health facilities and practitioners can provide referrals, outreach clinics, and maternal health services.
Our Work
The centers are meant to give mothers and guardians knowledge and skills that will help them build more stable lives. Informed and economically empowered mothers make choices that strengthen whole households. The centers will also provide secure, supervised play spaces where children who are safe, well fed, healthy, and stimulated in their early years are better able to learn, stay in school, and grow into productive adults. For orphans and children from the most fragile households, the center may be the one consistent, caring place in their day.

Investing in early childhood and in mothers is among the most effective ways to improve a community’s long-term prospects. In Uganda, cities are growing fast. Much of that growth happens in peri-urban slums—overcrowded, under-served neighborhoods with cramped housing, poor sanitation, and stretched or absent public services. On the edges of Kampala lie informal settlements, where irregular meals and limited access to clinics leave children vulnerable to malnutrition and preventable illness that can affect their development for life. Schools and educators support learning and ease children’s transition into formal education.
What We Need
We need financial support to let the first centers open. We also need to rely on a network of partners to extend what each center can do. Without this support, programs that communities see as their own are far more likely to last. Programs that depend entirely on outside funding and staff tend to fade when support ends.

The origins of the border collie
Border collies are a working dog shaped by a working-over-looks ethos, unlike many breeds refined around a show-ring standard. They were shaped by the needs of the people who worked them, and those needs were very specific.
Shepherds tended their flocks across open hillsides where a straying animal could mean real loss. Drovers moved livestock over long distances to markets. The dog that could herd was bred; appearance did not save a dog that couldn’t.
Adam Telfer was a Northumberland shepherd working in the 19th century. He paired dogs with the working qualities he wanted to strengthen. Early dogs were regional working collies, not a standardized breed. Sheepdog trials began in the 19th century and remain popular.
The history of the border collie: a working dog
Adam Telfer and others like him bred the border collie, but the dog’s herding precision was shaped over centuries in hard country by people who needed working dogs. The breed’s origins lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17th through 19th centuries.

Historical accounts of early breeding are patchy, so finer details should be held loosely. But one thing is clear: Border collies have a working dog history, not a show-ring history. That makes a difference.
The way we think about our dogs’ behavior has changed over the years. Our understanding of how dogs think and what they need has evolved. But when we look back at the way dogs have been bred over the years, we can see the mark of the breeding standards that were in place at the time. Border collies are an exception. How border collies herd
Border collies herd by using behaviors that are modified pieces of the predatory sequence found in wolves and other canids. Dogs can be taught to do a lot of things, but their basic instincts are still there. Border collies herd by using orient, eye, stalk, chase.
Orient: The dog orients toward the sheep and determines what the sheep are doing.
Eye: The dog fixates on the sheep, staring at them and holding their attention.
Stalk: The dog moves in a low, deliberate approach, moving the sheep through presence rather than force.
Chase: The dog chases the sheep.
In border collies, the grab-and-kill end of the predatory sequence has been largely bred out. The dog can’t chase and grab unless it’s been specifically taught to do so. But the first three behaviors—orient, eye, stalk—are still there. And that’s where the breed’s herding precision comes from. It’s been shaped over centuries in hard country

This is the quintessential sheepdog: the border collie. They’re a breed that comes in a wide range of coat types, colors, ear carriages, and sizes. But one thing they all have in common is that they are bred to work and, no matter how much they live in your house, their drive doesn’t switch off. That’s something Patricia McConnell, a certified applied animal behaviorist and working border collie owner, has emphasized.
“They need a lot of exercise—mental, too, not just physical,” McConnell says. “They’re not a dog for everyone.”
Border collies have an intense eye that is a fixed stare that exerts pressure on livestock without physical contact. They run the early steps of the predatory sequence with extraordinary refinement. But one end of the sequence, the grab-and-kill end, has been largely bred out of them.
“The ideal working border collie has the perfect mixture of balance—the ability to find the exact right point in space and put the exact right amount of pressure on the sheep—and power,” McConnell says. “Descendants of Telfer’s dogs became the foundation of the modern breed, and later celebrated herding dogs trace back to this lineage.”
The origins of the breed lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17th through 19th centuries. In those times, dogs that could think independently, endure bad weather, and read animal movement earned their keep and passed on their traits. A dog that could herd was bred, and appearance didn’t save a dog that couldn’t herd.
“It’s hard to get a clear picture of how the border collie breed evolved because historical accounts of early breeding are patchy,” McConnell says. “But here’s what we do know: the cross of a rough-coated collie and a borzoi produced a dog named Old Hemp, who became the progenitor of the border collie breed. A variety of factors (environment, genetics, selection, etc.) led to the development of this breed. One factor that wasn’t a part of the equation? Appearance.”
The variety of appearances in border collies reflects breeders who cared above all about ability. They come in a wide range of colors—black and white is the classic color, but merles, reds, tricolors, and others also occur.
But as herding dogs, border collies can work any type of stock, including sheep, cattle, poultry, and pigs. They can thrive in a home, but they need more than a daily walk. They may fixate on cars, bicycles, joggers, or children, and nip at the heels of family members, especially kids.
The best way to ensure that you and your border collie have a happy life together is to research the breed thoroughly before you adopt. And don’t forget, McConnell says, “A dog that could herd was bred; appearance did not save a dog that couldn’t herd.”

Our Curriculum
The Faith is the lens through which every subject in the Consensus Curriculum is taught. The Catholic worldview shapes the way students approach literature, history, science, and the arts. As a result, our students are better able to approach the world and its wonders with a sense of wonder at the order of creation, or to open questions about conscience, sacrifice, and redemption through a novel, or to look for the good in history or the beauty and creativity in music and visual art.
The Consensus Curriculum is designed to help students grow intellectually, spiritually, and as men and women of faith. The intellectual goals of the curriculum are:
Mastery of foundational skills in reading, writing, mathematics, and scientific reasoning, built progressively from early grades through middle school.
Moral reasoning – applying knowledge to real decisions about how to live.
Effective written and spoken communication – expressing ideas with clarity and charity.
Technology and Information Literacy – responsible, ethical, and effective use of digital tools.
The Consensus Curriculum is not a one-size-fits-all list of content. It is a framework that allows teachers to plan carefully, use varied methods, assess progress, and adjust when students need more support or more challenge.
Students learn from their teachers. They learn from the way a teacher treats a struggling classmate, handles a conflict, or responds to a hard question. It is not enough that teachers be skilled in their subject area; they must be both skilled and faithful. They serve as witnesses to the faith as well as content experts.
The Faith and the Family
The Church teaches that parents are the primary educators of their children. As a result, principals must lead both academically and spiritually. They serve as both the instructional leader and the spiritual leader of the school community. As instructional leaders, principals ensure the curriculum is implemented, observe classrooms, support teachers’ professional growth, review student progress, and see that standards translate into real learning. As spiritual leaders, principals shape a school culture where prayer, sacraments, service, and Catholic identity are lived realities.

This suggested visit is designed to take less than an hour. Start at the memorial fountain, then follow the streets down to the cathedral and Telford’s bridge. The people of Dunkeld chose a fountain – a structure that delivers water – as the memorial to the Duke rather than a statue. They recognised the water supply as a practical improvement to daily life and marked it in stone. The stone fountain stands in the middle of the square, commemorating George Murray, 6th Duke of Atholl who died in 1864. The Atholl estate played a leading part in the rebuilding and later improvements and its stewardship of the cathedral grounds helped preserve the site.
Dunkeld was an important ecclesiastical centre in early medieval Scotland. The cathedral dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries but after the Reformation it fell into partial ruin. Much of the land and property around it came under the family’s control over time. The Atholl seat was Blair Castle, to the north of Dunkeld, and the family’s influence over the town grew as old church structures lost authority. The ducal family’s decisions could affect housing and the village school in a small town. The estate shaped the street layout, the setting of the cathedral and the wider landscape around the town. The 4th Duke is known as the ‘Planter Duke’ for planting vast numbers of larches and other conifers across Atholl lands. The woodlands around Dunkeld still bear the mark of these plantings.
The Murrays held land across this part of Perthshire for centuries. In 1689, after the Battle of Killiecrankie, Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment fought in Dunkeld and much of the town burned. It was rebuilt over the following decades and the town’s centre now has whitewashed cottages with neat gables and a cathedral by the water. The bridge replaced ferries and gave the town a lasting connection to the south. It is one of the most photographed views in the area, with the cathedral and river behind it. Dunkeld cathedral in its present form dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. It was used as the cathedral choir and remained in use as the parish church while the ruined nave stood beside it.
The Atholl estate provided work in forestry, farming and property maintenance and supported local institutions. The Little Houses hint at the modest vernacular architecture of the post-fire town. The buildings are a row of small, sturdy cottages restored in the twentieth century by the National Trust for Scotland.

This is your chance to make a difference, even if you don’t shop exclusively at farmers’ markets or use every scrap of food you buy.
By making a few simple swaps in your household, you can reduce waste and save money. And if you get the whole family in on it, you’ll be teaching them good habits, too.
1. Food
Food that lasts longer means fewer wasted dollars in the trash. You don’t have to shop exclusively at farmers’ markets, but shift a part of your grocery habits to local, in-season food. You’ll find that seasonal produce is often cheaper because it’s plentiful. (It’s also generally tastier.) Shopping at a farmers’ market, farm stand or the “local” section of your grocery store means buying fresh produce that won’t have to be shipped from across the country or the world.
2. Paper
Think about how long you use household paper such as grocery lists, to-do lists, phone messages and reminders — a few hours, tops — before it’s thrown away. You can replace it all with a dry-erase board. One board can replace thousands of sheets of paper over its lifetime. A magnetic board on the fridge works well, too. Photograph your grocery list before you leave the house to remove the need for a paper copy.
3. Batteries
You use disposable batteries in remotes, game controllers, wireless mice, kids’ toys, flashlights and smoke detectors. But a single rechargeable battery can be reused hundreds of times, replacing a pile of disposables. Rechargeable nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries plus a charger can replace disposables.
4. Cleaning
You don’t need paper towels, disposable wipes and single-use spray bottles to clean your house. Microfiber cloths can replace most paper towels. They trap dust and grime well, often with just water, and can be machine-washed many times. Washable mop pads can replace disposable ones.
5. Transportation
Food transportation is usually a smaller share of food’s environmental footprint than how the food is produced. The goal isn’t to never buy food shipped from afar, but to shift part of your grocery habits to local, in-season food. You can also buy seasonal produce at a farmers’ market, farm stand or the “local” section of a grocery store.
6. Your car
A professional car wash is the eco-friendlier option. Many commercial car washes use high-pressure, low-volume equipment and water reclamation systems, which use much less fresh water per car than a typical home wash. It’s also better for your car, because washing in the driveway sends water, soap, brake dust, oil and road grime into the storm drain.
7. Getting organized
Shopping exclusively at farmers’ markets isn’t required to make a difference. Shifting part of your grocery habits to local, in-season food has benefits. In-season produce is often cheaper because it’s plentiful. You can find seasonal produce at a farmers’ market, farm stand or the “local” section of a grocery store.
8. Laundry
Buy a laundry detergent in a concentrate and a reusable bottle, rather than a ready-to-use bottle. Concentrates are usually much cheaper per use.
9. Keeping it clean
Don’t just ditch paper towels. Cut back. Keep a roll of paper towels for truly messy jobs, but the goal is to cut back. Use washable mop pads instead of disposable ones. Use microfiber cloths to replace most paper towels. They trap dust and grime well, often with just water, and can be machine-washed many times.
10. Staying organized
A dry-erase board means buying far fewer notepads and sticky-note packs. A single board can replace thousands of sheets of paper over its lifetime. Photograph your grocery list before you leave the house to remove the need for a paper copy.

With the holidays approaching, there is a good chance you're thinking about ways you can help the environment. Perhaps you already recycle, buy reusable water bottles, donate items instead of throwing them away. There are plenty of ways to do good for the earth, and they don't take much time out of your day.
Here are some simple swaps you can make to help the environment — and they will make your life easier, too.
- Cleaning sheets such as Swiffer mop and duster sheets and Clorox wipes
- Sticky notes
- Rechargeable batteries
- Paper products such as grocery lists, to-do lists, phone messages and reminders
- Washing your car in the driveway
- Food waste
- Paper towels
- Seasonal produce
Each of these swaps only takes a few minutes to set up, but then becomes routine.
- Buy locally
Whether it's at a farmers' market, farm stand or the "local" section of your grocery store, seasonal produce is healthier to consume than food that has to travel long distances to get to you. Keep in mind that many of the products you buy from a farmers' market will not be certified organic, but if you visit a farm stand, you can find out how the food is grown. Farmers markets are also a great way to meet people in your community and support local businesses.
- Replace paper towels with microfiber cloths
Microfiber cloths can replace most of your paper towels, trapping dust and grime well — often with just water. They can also be machine-washed many times, so you can use them over and over again. Keep a small basket under your sink to hold used cloths and let them go in with your regular laundry.
- Use rechargeable batteries
A single rechargeable battery can be reused hundreds of times, replacing a pile of disposables. Modern "low self-discharge" NiMH batteries hold their charge for months in a drawer and work in low-drain devices, so you don't have to keep the charger where you used to store spare batteries. Once you get in the habit of swapping in charged batteries, you'll never go back.
- Replace Swiffer mop and duster sheets with reusable mops and refillable eco-friendly cleaning products
If you use products such as Swiffer mop and duster sheets or Clorox wipes, consider using reusable mops and refillable eco-friendly cleaning products instead. They are equally convenient and you'll keep large numbers of single-use cleaning sheets out of landfills.
- Use a dry-erase board
A dry-erase board stays in view so your notes are less likely to be misplaced. Instead of sticky notes, which are not easily recyclable because of their adhesive, write down your to-do lists, phone messages and reminders.
- Avoid washing your car in the driveway
When you wash your car in the driveway, you send water, soap, brake dust, oil and road grime into the storm drain. You can avoid this problem by washing your car at a car wash, where the water is treated before it enters the sewer system.
- Buy concentrates
Concentrates are usually much cheaper per use than ready-to-use bottles. And you'll be keeping less paper, plastic and packaging out of landfills.
- Compost your food waste
Food waste is one of the biggest household contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. You can help by composting your food waste instead of throwing it away. If you live in an apartment or condo, consider using a worm bin or bokashi system. If you have a yard, you can build or buy a compost bin or tumbler.

Most supply chains still have warehouses. But how do you know if yours is a useful tool or just overhead? Many executives treat them as a given, like loading docks or invoices. But warehouses are where goods wait, and waiting costs money. A warehouse must save more in freight, inventory risk, or service than it adds through handling and space. Start from function: ask what the facility does that would not happen otherwise. "We have always done it this way" is a warning.
Here are four classic functions that cover most legitimate reasons for a warehouse. Information provision supports them.
Break-bulk: Does the customer need smaller quantities than the supplier ships, and is it cheaper to move the bulk to one point first? A warehouse that breaks down goods into smaller lots is the reverse of a consolidation warehouse, which gathers goods from many suppliers and combines them into one shipment for the customer. Consolidation can reduce freight costs and the number of deliveries a customer must receive and process. But if you fail the consolidation test — i.e., if combining goods doesn’t give meaningful savings in freight — then you can fail the break-bulk test, too. For example, an office-supplies center failed break-bulk because the goods arrived in customer-ready quantities, so there was nothing to break down.
Customization: Is there work that is cheaper or more flexible to do close to the customer than at the factory? If you have no on-site value-added work, you can fail customization. For example, an office-supplies center failed customization because there was no on-site kitting, labeling, or special packaging.
Storage: Is there a genuine timing mismatch between supply and demand, and is it cheaper to hold stock than suffer stockouts or expedited shipping? Seasonal products, long production runs, and uncertain demand justify holding inventory close to the customer. For example, an office-supplies center failed storage because demand was stable and predictable, and inventory turned over quickly.
Consolidation: Does the customer buy from many sources, and does combining items into fewer, fuller shipments save more than the extra handling costs? A facility that fails every test is overhead, not a strategic asset. For example, a center failed consolidation because combining goods gave no meaningful freight savings, and it failed storage because demand was stable and predictable. Even though demand was steady, the agency might have justified a warehouse because demand is not seasonal, perishable, or speculative, so there was no real buffer to hold against a surge or shortage. But the center didn’t assemble mixed shipments from many distant sources in a way that cut freight costs, so it failed the consolidation test. The extra handling meant extra labor, extra space, extra inventory on the balance sheet, and extra days in lead time.
A non-profit organization supplied office products to its member agencies: paper, pens, toner, folders, and similar staples. Suppliers shipped products to the center, the center stored them, and staff picked orders and shipped them to the agencies. The agencies received the same products they could have received directly from the supplier, but later and at higher cost.
The sensible answer in this case was elimination. Have suppliers ship directly to the agencies, or use a distributor that already offers consolidated delivery. In any case, the center failed every function test.
But many executives treat warehouses as a given, like loading docks or invoices. The mere existence of a central facility suggests control, predictable availability, and a single point of contact. By delaying differentiation, you reduce the risk of holding the wrong variety of product. But if you fail the functions tests, you have a facility that fails every test — not a strategic asset.
A distribution center earns its keep when it breaks bulk, smooths timing, consolidates freight, or customizes product in ways that reduce total cost or improve service. If your warehouse fails the tests, you can be confident that you can do without it.

High blood pressure is called “the silent killer” because it can cause organ damage years before it causes symptoms. The only way to know for sure if you have it is to get it checked. It’s one of the simplest first steps toward preventing cardiovascular disease.
Home checking takes only a few minutes, and it can reveal a risk factor years before it causes harm. Even if your blood pressure is fine, home monitoring shows how it behaves across your ordinary days, away from the stress of the clinic.
For diagnosed high blood pressure or if your doctor requests you monitor your blood pressure, take readings for about seven days before a medical appointment or after a medication change. You will get a reliable baseline from this week of readings that will be more informative than any single number.
Morning measurement
- within an hour of waking
- after using the bathroom
- before eating, drinking coffee, exercising, or taking blood pressure medication
Evening measurement
- before dinner or before bed
- at roughly the same time each day
Upper-arm automatic monitors are generally more accurate than wrist or finger devices. Most come with a standard cuff; larger or smaller sizes are sold separately. Check the size of the cuff by measuring around the middle of your upper arm and compare with the size range printed on the cuff or in the manual.
Place the cuff on bare skin, not over clothing. The bottom edge of the cuff should sit about an inch above the bend of the elbow, with the tubing running along the inside of the arm. A rolled-up sleeve should not act as a tourniquet. Sit in a chair with a back, with your back straight and against the chair. Rest your arm on a table or desk, with the middle of the cuff at heart level. Sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring without talking, scrolling a phone, or watching something stressful. Measure at the same times each day so the readings are comparable. A full bladder can raise the reading, so empty it beforehand. If your blood pressure is very high without symptoms, rest five minutes and measure again; if still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
If you have symptoms of a heart attack or stroke, seek urgent medical attention if your reading is 180/120 or higher, especially if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or difficulty speaking. If your blood pressure is very high but you don’t have any symptoms, rest five minutes and measure again; if still that high, contact your doctor promptly.

High blood pressure is a serious health issue, raising your risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and heart failure. But you can monitor your blood pressure at home and get a warning years before it causes harm. Here’s what you need to know about home blood pressure monitoring.
First, the basics. Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of arteries. High blood pressure, or hypertension, occurs when the force is too high. The normal blood pressure for most adults is below 120/80 mm Hg. But over 100 million Americans have high blood pressure.
High blood pressure raises your risk of cardiovascular disease. That’s why it’s important to find out whether you have high blood pressure and how high it is. Blood pressure taken at the end of the day is higher because you’ve been moving around and the day’s stress is still with you. For that reason, most doctors recommend measuring your blood pressure in the morning when you first wake up. Take it within an hour of waking, after you’ve used the bathroom, and before you eat, drink coffee, exercise, or take your blood pressure medication.
How to take your blood pressure
Follow the instructions that come with the monitor. Here are the basics.
- Rest your arm on a table or desk, so that the middle of the cuff is at heart level.
- Slide the cuff onto your arm, with the bottom under your clothing and just above the elbow.
- Stay still and quiet while the device inflates.
- Take two to three readings each time you test your blood pressure.
A single reading in your doctor’s office is just a snapshot. It’s important to have a monitoring schedule that fits your health condition and your monitoring needs. You’ll need to know how often to measure, what time of day, and how to do it. Your healthcare provider can advise on the schedule and targets suited to you.
Most people are advised to measure their blood pressure at home in the morning, when they first wake up. But your doctor may want you to check your blood pressure at other times as well. If you check too often, however, it can fuel your anxiety and cause you to overreact to normal fluctuations. So talk to your doctor about the right frequency for your situation.
A week of readings gives you a reliable baseline that’s more informative than any single number. If you’re new to home monitoring, consider picking up a validated monitor, setting aside a week, and sharing your results with your healthcare provider.
Home blood pressure monitoring
It’s easy to monitor your blood pressure at home. It takes only a few minutes, and you can find out about a risk factor years before it causes harm. But you need to be careful and follow the instructions that come with your monitor.
Follow these steps to get an accurate reading.
- Place your feet flat on the floor with your legs uncrossed.
- Rest your arm on a table or desk, so that the middle of the cuff is at heart level. (If you hold your arm above heart level, you’ll get a falsely low reading. If you hold your arm below heart level, you’ll get a falsely high reading.)
- Slide the cuff onto your arm with the bottom under your clothing and just above your elbow.
- Stay still and quiet while the device inflates.
- Record your readings so you can share them with your doctor. (Don’t diagnose or adjust your medication on your own. Bring the log with you to your appointment so your doctor can see the full pattern.)
Most devices come with a standard cuff, but if you need a larger or smaller size, you can purchase those separately. When you use the right size cuff, the results are more accurate.
To make sure that your home blood pressure monitor is a tool for protecting your heart, brain, and kidneys, follow these steps:
- Make sure you’re consistent with your timing, rest, and sitting.
- Make sure you’re using the right size cuff.
- Keep a log and share your results with your doctor.
Home blood pressure monitoring is a quick and easy way to find out whether you have high blood pressure. It’s a way to reveal a risk factor years before it causes harm.

Cropland extent products are crucial for developing higher-level cropland products such as cropping intensities, crop types, crop watering methods (irrigated or rainfed), crop productivity, and crop water productivity. Croplands are defined by what they do over time as well as by their appearance on a single date. Thus, repeated mapping over time reveals cropland expansion, abandonment, and conversion to urban use. Repeated mapping allows us to not only map the cropland extent but also to develop products that can measure the performance of these croplands. For example, we can estimate total cropland area as well as the crop types, crop watering methods, crop productivity, and crop water productivity. Cropland extent products are especially crucial in countries such as Australia and China where water allocation is a constant concern and groundwater depletion is a serious issue (in northern China) respectively. Cropland extent products are usually derived from medium resolution data (e.g., 30-m), however, reference samples are costly to collect over large areas. Therefore, classification using a pixel-based supervised random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) executed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform has been used in this study to develop a Landsat 30-m derived cropland extent product for Australia and China. This study developed a Landsat 30-m derived cropland extent product for Australia and China. The Landsat data covered the years 2013–2015 and were time-composited over 4–6 time-periods per year using median value for various agro-ecological zones (AEZs) of Australia and China. The random forest MLA generated new cropland extent maps for Australia and China. The data products are freely available from the USGS website at https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/node/1282. The croplands versus non-croplands knowledge base for training the RF algorithm was derived from the MFDC. The overall accuracy of the cropland extent product for Australia was 97.6% with 98.8% producer's accuracy and 79% user's accuracy. The cropland product for Australia had an overall accuracy of 97.6%, with 98.8% producer's accuracy and 79% user's accuracy. This memorial fountain is in Dunkeld, on the site of the Market Cross. The fountain was erected in 1866 to commemorate George Murray, 6th Duke of Atholl, who died in 1864. The water supply to Dunkeld's homes was a gift from the Atholl estate, but the water is not of drinking quality. The estate played a leading part in the rebuilding and later improvements after much of the town burned in 1689 after the Battle of Killiecrankie. Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment fought in Dunkeld and much of the town burned. Much of the town was re-built after the Battle of Dunkeld (1689) and much of the woodlands around the town still bear the mark of these plantings.

Simple everyday ways to help the environment
Here are a few simple tips that you can apply to your everyday life to help the environment.
1. Buy Local and Seasonal Food. Buying local and seasonal food often means less packaging, less refrigerated storage time and less spoilage before it reaches the buyer. Also, locally sourced food is healthier to consume. Many grocery stores carry local foods and often post signs near them saying they are local. Many grocery stores carry local foods and often post signs near them saying they are local. In many areas storm drains carry runoff untreated to local streams, rivers and lakes. By not washing your car at home, you can keep these chemicals out of local streams, rivers and lakes.
2. Buy Rechargeable Batteries. Used in remotes, game controllers, wireless mice, kids' toys, flashlights and smoke detectors, disposable batteries can leach harmful materials if not disposed of properly. Make the simple switch to rechargeable batteries. Buy packs in the most commonly used battery sizes and swap them in when your current batteries run low.
3. Buy Reusable Mops and Refillable Eco-Friendly Cleaning Products. Single-use cleaning products and tools (Swiffer mop and duster sheets, Clorox wipes) contain toxic chemicals, such as ethyl alcohol, Alkyl Polyglucoside, and Didecyl Dimethyl Ammonium Chloride. Reusable mops and refillable eco-friendly cleaning products are better for the environment and your home.

That doesn’t mean there’s nothing you can do to help. Even the simplest actions can make a difference. And if your environmental contributions can also be simple and practical, all the better. If you need ideas to get you started, here are a few:
Use rechargeable batteries
Rechargeable batteries cost a little more upfront, but they save you money over time. They also reduce the amount of hazardous waste that ends up in landfills. It’s a simple switch: buy packs in the most commonly used battery sizes and swap them in when current batteries run low.
Clean with reusable tools
Single-use cleaning products and tools like Swiffer mop and duster sheets and Clorox wipes are convenient, but when you consider large numbers of these single-use cleaning sheets piling up in landfills, they’re not good for the environment. Reusable mops and refillable eco-friendly cleaning products are equally convenient alternatives. You’ll also reduce the amount of toxic chemicals like ethyl alcohol, Alkyl Polyglucoside, and Didecyl Dimethyl Ammonium Chloride that end up in landfills.
Buy local
Food is currently shipped from all over the world. When you buy from local growers and farmers, it requires less energy for the transportation of food. Local farmers markets are one way to buy local food. And many grocery stores carry local foods. Often, they post signs near them saying they are local. This means you’re also consuming healthier food.
Avoid washing your car
Car washes generally use much less water than you would if you were to wash your car yourself. They also use high-powered machines to clean cars quickly and efficiently. And some car washes will also vacuum the inside of your car.

A dry-erase board stays in view so you’re less likely to misplace notes. It’s a great way to replace notepads and post-it notes for to-do lists, grocery lists, and family notes. You’ll also reduce the amount of waste.
A few simple changes can have a big impact. There are lots of ways to make a difference, even if you don’t have time to make a big environmental contribution.

How Often to Measure
At the very least, your blood pressure should be checked once every year at a doctor visit. If you have high blood pressure, you should check more frequently. Talk to your doctor about how often you should be measuring based on your health history. If you have hypertension, you may need to check twice a day until your blood pressure is under control. Once you’ve got your blood pressure under control, you can reduce the frequency of testing, while continuing to monitor your heart health.

Our German and Te Reo programmes are designed to help our students stand with confidence on a local marae or order a meal in a Berlin café. That means that at different stages, the programmes have different focuses and goals. In Year 10 for example, the Te Reo focus is formal language and marae tikanga, while the German focus is travel and everyday situations. The main goals of both programmes are to prepare students for NCEA Level 1 by correspondence, to give them a foundation for travel to German speaking countries if they wish, and to ensure that we always have a close liaison with our local marae.
German (Years 7-8)
Our German programme runs from Year 7 through to Year 10. In Year 7 and 8, we begin with an introduction to basic vocabulary and key phrases, learning to count to 100 and say the German alphabet. We also cover the basic geography of Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Year 7 and 8 students have a Te Reo lesson once a week for two terms, and learn to introduce themselves, talk about their family, age, birthday, where they are from and their house. In the second year they build on their language knowledge from the previous year, learning to talk about school subjects, pets, hobbies, sport, food and how to tell the time.
German (Years 9-10)
In Year 9 our programme builds on the basics covered in the junior school. In the odd year, our focus is on Te Marae (the marae), and our students learn to count to 100 and say the German alphabet. In the second year, we build on the language knowledge from the previous year, and our students learn to talk about school subjects, pets, hobbies, sport, food and how to tell the time. Year 9 students have two periods of Te Reo for two terms, and in the third Term, they have 3 German lessons a week. We extend our students’ vocabulary, using the computer programme ‘Languagenut’ to help them learn vocabulary. Our Year 10 German programme helps to create a foundation for students wishing to study German in Year 10. Our students continue to learn about the similarities and differences between German and New Zealand culture, and we teach them about accommodation and directions, travel and transport.
Te Reo Māori (Year 10)
Te Reo Māori is an option in Year 10. Our Year 10 Te Reo Māori programme is designed to prepare students with confidence and skill to study NCEA Level 1 by correspondence. Our focus in Year 10 is on formal language, marae tikanga, including pōwhiri (welcome ceremonies), roles on the marae and appropriate behaviour. We also study tikanga of the marae, including describing people, places and events in more detail. Students leave with lasting skills: confidence in speaking, respect for other cultures, and a stronger connection to their own community.

Our German programme is available to students in years 7 and 8. Lessons take place twice a week for a third of the year and focuses on building a foundation to students wishing to study German at an NCEA level. Students are introduced to German life and culture through the Ministry of Education’s ‘Ja’ series. They learn to count to 100 and say the German alphabet. They also learn to introduce themselves, talk about their family, age, birthday, where they are from, and their house. Students also learn to talk about the school subjects, pets, hobbies, sport, food, and how to tell the time. In the second year students continue to learn about differences and similarities between New Zealand and German culture. They also build on language knowledge from the previous year. The key aim of the programme is to introduce students to another language and culture.
Our Te Reo programme is available to students in years 7 to 10. In year 7 and 8, Te Reo is offered to students once a week for two terms. Students work on the basics covered in the junior school. They focus on sentence structure and simple conversations. In year 10, Te Reo is an option. Students who choose to study Te Reo have two periods a week for the full year. They work more formally using the text books Te Reo Take Take and Te Matapuna. Students have the opportunity to build their confidence and skill to study NCEA Level 1 by correspondence. In year 9, Te Reo is also offered to students. Students have 3 lessons of Te Reo for 2 terms. One group focuses on Matariki and the second group studies Parihaka.
